summary: Octagonal blue-limestone light on Lake Champlain north of Plattsburgh, built in 1858 and replaced by a buoy in 1989. The tower is closed to visitors.

structures.note: Cape Cod style cottage attached to the tower; moved a short way north in 1934 and used as a private residence

access.note: Tower and grounds closed to the public. Permission needed from the owners of the land next to the station. The tower can be seen through the trees from Point Au Roche Road.

events.note: Congress appropriated $5,000 for a light at the point; the government bought 10.4 acres from Nathan Perry for $440
Temporary beacon exhibited from the point until the lighthouse began operation
Station established (US Lighthouse Society); LighthouseFriends gives 1859 for activation, see notes
LighthouseFriends: not activated until the opening of navigation in 1859
Barn and stable erected for the keeper
Cistern built in the dwelling's cellar
Tower deck and coping repainted inside and out
Grover C. Oliver placed in charge
Electric light installed atop the tower (LighthouseFriends)
Town of Beekmantown gives 1934; LighthouseFriends dates the electric light to 1933
Most of the property sold for $2,100 to Grover C. Oliver, a former keeper
Replaced by a buoy on La Roche Reef; the Coast Guard judged the tower unsafe (LighthouseFriends); the GSA declared the lighthouse obsolete (Town)

notes_for_editor: Dates: the record and the USLHS say 1858 for the tower and lens; LighthouseFriends says the light was not activated until 1859, after a temporary beacon from 1856. No Lighthouse Board report from the 1850s or 1860s is in our corpus (the corpus holds Light-House Board reports only for 1891 to 1901), so the 1852 appropriation, the 1856 beacon and the 1859 activation rest on LighthouseFriends alone; a human should check the 1850s annual reports. Ownership: LighthouseFriends (Coast Guard owns the tower), the Town (privately owned now) and Cyberlights (GSA seeking transfer to the Town, page last visited 2002) disagree; the story says so. Automation: the Town gives 1934 and LighthouseFriends the electric light of 1933. Land kept in 1934: the Town says 50 square feet, LighthouseFriends a fifty-foot-square lot. Range: the sources say 13 miles without saying statute or nautical; range_nm is left empty. Focal height: Wikipedia gives 59 ft (18 m), which the story does not use; USLHS, the Town and LighthouseFriends give 54 ft. The keeper roster is the USLHS roster (the roster tool notes it comes from NARA keeper registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory; each name should be confirmed in a primary record before publication); LighthouseFriends lists the same names and years. The Fire Island Light link (us-ny-fire-island) assumes LighthouseFriends's 'Fire Island Lighthouse' is that station, which is the 1826 light; please confirm. Bailey's 1928 report is known only as LighthouseFriends quotes it; the story says so. Newspapers: no Chronicling America hit on the station in New York papers; one broad search found nothing relevant. The USCG Historian's archived page was not available (Wayback returned 404). The 1893 Light-House Board entry is cited by scan page only; its printed page was not confirmed. The 1899 printed page 77 is from the report's running head.
